title: AAWSAP set up to take a Lockheed-held UFO; transfer killed
summary: Jesse Michels tells of AAWSAP set up to take a Lockheed-held UFO; transfer killed, about an unknown time at Las Vegas, Nevada, and relays what a named person told them. As told, not a fact.

tellings.quote: so ASAP was actually set up to transfer a UFO held by locking Martin to a special Access program to get some Outsider civilian scientist eyes on it
the person involved in transferring this UFO to ASAP was VP of locking Martin Space Systems Advanced Technology Center a guy named Jim Ryder
tellings.difference: Names Jim Ryder, VP of Lockheed Martin Space Systems Advanced Technology Center, as the person involved in the transfer, and does not mention the transfer being killed.
tellings.link_reason: Both tell of the plan to move a UFO held by Lockheed Martin into AAWSAP. This telling names the Lockheed executive said to be involved in the transfer.

as_told.title: Lockheed tries to transfer Kingman material to OSAP in 2008

plain: AAWSAP was a Pentagon-funded study of unexplained phenomena, run through the Defense Intelligence Agency with Bigelow Aerospace, a company in Las Vegas. The podcast host Jesse Michels says it was set up so that a UFO held by the aerospace company Lockheed Martin could be moved into a special access program, a tightly restricted secret program, so that outside civilian scientists could study it. If true, a private contractor has been holding a craft that was never shown to outsiders. Michels names Jim Ryder, a vice president at a Lockheed Martin space technology centre, as the man involved in the handover, and says the craft was collected in the 1950s. He says a CIA official, Glenn Gaffney, was the gatekeeper and blocked the transfer, citing an article by a writer named Chris Sharp. A physicist, Eric Davis, says Gaffney was hostile to the company releasing its collection of crash-retrieval material, kept since before a program shut down in 1989, though he doesn't name the company. Ross Coulthart ties the story to a 2017 New York Times article by Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal and suggests the craft may come from a crash in Kingman in 1953.
